problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+y=0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?
worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+1=0.
$$

 

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\lambda =\pm \text{i}$ are the purely imaginary roots of the auxiliary equation. 

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{\text{i}x})=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{\text{i}x})=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ is not a solution.
